papers.title: Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae , with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment ( n = 166), M segment ( n = 48), and S segment ( n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L ( R 2 = 0.069), M ( R 2 = 0.021), and S ( R 2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular-clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus -associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa.

Keywords: African hantaviruses, Phylogenomics, Orthohantavirus, One Health, Virus-host co-divergence, Zoonotic surveillance Introduction Emerging zoonotic viruses, including hantaviruses, continue to pose significant threats to global public health [1,2]. Africa is recognized as a hotspot for pathogen emergence because of its exceptional biodiversity, rapid environmental change, and increasing human–wildlife interactions [3]. Although considerable attention has focused on high-profile viral haemorrhagic fevers such as Ebola virus disease and Lassa fever, the diversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of many other zoonotic viruses remain poorly understood. Among these neglected pathogens are hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae), which were historically regarded as rodent-borne viruses distributed predominantly across Europe, Asia, and the Americas [1].. However, increasing molecular surveillance over the past two decades has demonstrated that hantaviruses are also widely distributed throughout Africa and circulate in diverse mammalian hosts, revealing substantially broader evolutionary and ecological diversity than previously recognized [4,5]. Members of the family Hantaviridae are enveloped viruses with a tripartite, negative- sense, single-stranded RNA genome comprising the Small (S), Medium (M), and Large (L) segments, which encode the nucleocapsid protein, glycoprotein precursor, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, respectively [6]. Hantaviruses were traditionally considered highly host-associated viruses that evolved predominantly in rodents through long-term virus–host associations [7,8]. However, the discovery of genetically divergent hantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats substantially expanded this paradigm and demonstrated that the evolutionary diversity of the family extends across multiple mammalian orders [5,9]. These discoveries are particularly relevant to Africa, which represents an important but underexplored reservoir of hantavirus diversity, harbouring diverse ecosystems and mammalian hosts that remain incompletely characterized [10,11]. The discovery of Sangassou virus in the African wood mouse (Hylomyscus simus) in Guinea provided the first molecular evidence of an indigenous African rodent- associated hantavirus and established that African rodents harbour evolutionarily distinct viral lineages [6,12]. Subsequent investigations expanded the known diversity through the identification of Tanganya virus and Bowe virus in Crocidura shrews in Guinea [9], Azagny virus in the West African pygmy shrew (Crocidura obscurior) in Côte d'Ivoire [13], and highly divergent hantaviruses in banana pipistrelle bats (Neoromicia nanus) from Côte d'Ivoire [14]. Rodent-, shrew-, and bat-associated hantaviruses have subsequently been reported from Gabon, Sierra Leone, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Egypt, Senegal, Benin, and, more recently, Mali, highlighting the substantial host and geographic diversity of African hantaviruses [15,16,17,18]. The increasing availability of viral genomic sequences has revealed pronounced host- associated and geographic structuring among African hantaviruses [19,20]. Previous phylogenetic investigations indicate that indigenous African hantaviruses comprise several deeply divergent evolutionary lineages associated with rodents, shrews, and bats, whereas Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), primarily associated with commensal Rattus species, exhibits broader phylogenetic relationships with globally distributed lineages [17]. These observations suggest that African hantavirus diversity comprises geographically structured endemic lineages alongside widely distributed commensal- rodent-associated viruses. Nevertheless, the evolutionary relationships among these lineages and the extent to which host association and geographic structure are conserved across genomic segments remain incompletely resolved because most previous studies have focused on individual virus species, single genomic segments, or restricted geographic regions. Understanding the evolutionary ecology of African hantaviruses is increasingly important because ecological disturbance, urbanization, agricultural intensification, climate variability, and habitat fragmentation are altering wildlife communities and potentially increasing opportunities for zoonotic spillover [3]. Human infection occurs predominantly through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, and retrospective serological investigations have provided evidence of human exposure in several African countries [4,6]. However, hantavirus infections remain poorly recognized in routine clinical practice because their nonspecific manifestations overlap with those of malaria, typhoid fever, Lassa fever, leptospirosis, and other endemic febrile illnesses [21]. Consequently, the burden of hantavirus infection in Africa is likely underestimated, particularly in countries such as Nigeria, where hantavirus diversity and human infection remain poorly characterized. The recent 2026 Andes virus outbreak associated with the M/V Hondius cruise ship further demonstrates the potential for hantaviruses to generate cross-border public-health events requiring multinational surveillance, laboratory investigation, contact tracing, and coordinated international responses [22]. These observations emphasize the need to strengthen hantavirus surveillance within broader One Health frameworks for emerging zoonotic disease detection and preparedness. The segmented genome of hantaviruses provides an important basis for investigating whether evolutionary patterns are consistently represented across different genomic regions. Because the L, M, and S segments encode proteins with distinct biological functions, they may experience different evolutionary constraints, rates of sequence change, and selective pressures [23,24]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and contains relatively conserved regions that can provide phylogenetic information across divergent lineages, whereas the M segment encodes the viral glycoprotein precursor involved in virus–host cell interactions and may exhibit substantial sequence variation among viral lineages. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein and provides an additional functionally distinct marker for resolving evolutionary relationships. Consequently, phylogenies reconstructed from individual genomic segments may differ in their ability to resolve deep and shallow evolutionary relationships, including geographic and host-associated lineages [11,23,24]. In addition, comparison of segment-specific phylogenies enables assessment of whether viral lineages share a common evolutionary history. Strong topological concordance among segment phylogenies supports a broadly shared evolutionary history, whereas phylogenetic incongruence may reflect genetic reassortment or other segment-specific evolutionary processes [25,26]. Reassortment can occur following co-infection of a host with genetically distinct viruses and may generate discordant evolutionary histories among genomic segments [6,26]. Comparative analysis across all three genomic segments is therefore important for distinguishing robust host- and geographic-associated evolutionary patterns from signals specific to individual genomic regions. Despite the increasing discovery of genetically diverse hantaviruses in Africa, a continent-wide comparative framework integrating evolutionary relationships, host associations, geographic structure, and genomic congruence remains limited [11,17,27]. In particular, the extent to which host- and geographic-associated phylogenetic patterns are concordantly recovered across the L, M, and S genomic segments remains poorly characterized at the continental scale. Addressing these gaps is important for understanding the evolutionary organization of African hantavirus diversity and for identifying genomic and ecological priorities for One Health surveillance. In the present study, we performed a continent-wide comparative phylogenomic analysis of African hantaviruses using the L, M, and S genomic segments. We analysed 281 full-length and partial coding sequences from 13 African countries together with representative global reference sequences to characterize host- associated and geographic structuring and assess phylogenetic congruence among genomic segments. Pairwise tanglegram analyses were used to assess topological congruence among the L, M, and S phylogenies and identify discordant relationships potentially consistent with reassortment. By integrating multi-segment phylogenetic evidence with reservoir-host and geographic information, this study establishes a continent-wide framework for understanding the evolutionary structure of African hantaviruses and provides a foundation for future genomic surveillance, One Health preparedness, and global health security. Materials and Methods Sequence dataset A total of 281 hantavirus nucleotide sequences representing the three genomic segments were analyzed: 48 M-segment, 67 S-segment, and 166 L-segment sequences (Supplementary Table 1). All sequences from Africa (Egypt, Senegal, Benin, Mali, Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Sierra Leone, Gabon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and Madagascar) were retrieved from National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank and represent isolates collected between 2004 and 2024 with no isolates from 2025 together with selected reference strains from Asia, Europe, and the Americas to provide global phylogenetic context. Sequence alignment Nucleotide sequences for each genomic segment (L, M, and S) were aligned independently using MAFFT v7 [28] with the --auto algorithm and otherwise default parameters. Alignments were inspected and manually edited in AliView v1.01 [29] to ensure positional homology. Ambiguously aligned regions and sites with excessive gaps were removed prior to phylogenetic inference. Phylogenetic inference Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenies for each segment were inferred using IQ- TREE v2.1.3 [30]. For each alignment the best-fit nucleotide substitution model was selected by ModelFinder [31] implemented within IQ-TREE. Node support was assessed with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates [32]. The ML trees files were exported in Newick format with branch lengths in substitutions/site and visualized in interactive Tree Of Life version 7.6 iTOL [33]. Assessment of temporal signal Temporal signal of each segment dataset was evaluated using Clockor2 v1.9.1 [34] (https://clockor2.github.io). ML trees with branch lengths in substitutions/site (Newick format) and sampling dates (from sequence metadata or CSV file) were used as inputs. Root-to-tip regression was performed independently for the L, M, and S datasets. The temporal signal was judged insufficient to support reliable molecular clock dating. Therefore, time-calibrated Bayesian phylogenetic analyses and molecular clock dating were not performed. Comparative phylogenetic analysis and detection of reassortment To ensure consistent taxon labels across segment datasets, isolates were assigned unique identifiers (HTV001–HTV198) and a mapping file linking identifiers to accession numbers and metadata is provided in Supplementary Table 1. Trees were rooted consistently by midpoint rooting in FigTree v1.4.4 [35]. Congruence among the L, M, and S genomic segments, ML trees were compared using Dendroscope v3.5.7 [36]. Pairwise tanglegrams (L–M, L–S, and M–S) were generated using the Tanglegram module; the built-in untangling algorithm was applied to minimize edge crossings while preserving topology. Trees used for tanglegrams were exported in NEXUS format. Putative reassortment events were identified by examining isolates that occupied incongruent phylogenetic positions between paired segment trees. Particular attention was given to taxa that clustered within different evolutionary lineages while maintaining strong branch support in the original phylogenetic analyses. Given that topological discordance may also arise from incomplete phylogenetic resolution, stochastic error, or differences in evolutionary histories among genomic segments, putative reassortment events were interpreted conservatively by integrating tanglegram patterns with branch support, host species, geographic origin, and the broader phylogenetic context. Results Dataset Characteristics We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the three hantavirus genomic segments: L, encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (n = 166), M, encoding the glycoprotein precursor (n = 48), and S, encoding the nucleocapsid protein (n = 67) (Supplementary Table 1). The dataset comprised sequences from 13 African countries spanning West n= 70, Central n=2, East n=46, and North Africa n= 16 and Madagascar n=91, together with representative global reference strains (supplementary table 1). African sequences were derived from diverse mammalian hosts, including rodents, shrews, and bats, allowing comparative assessment of host-associated and geographic phylogenetic structure. Assessment of Temporal Signal Root-to-tip regression showed weak temporal structure for the L, M and S datasets (R2 = 0.069, 0.021 and 0.046, respectively), indicating insufficient temporal signal for reliable molecular-clock inference. Consequently, time-calibrated phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses were not undertaken. Subsequent evolutionary comparisons were therefore based on phylogenetic topology, branch support, host association, and geographic distribution rather than divergence-time estimates. Continent-wide Multi-Segment Phylogenomic Study of Host and Geographic Structuring of African Hantaviruses. 1Mkpuma Nicodemus*, 1Oyekan Olumuyiwa, 1Igah Lanre, 2Uwem Okon Edet, 1Adedeji Jeremy Adeyinka,1Meseko Adebajo Clement Author’s Affiliation 1National Veterinary Research Institute, Vom, Nigeria 2Department of Microbiology, School of Pure and Applied Sciences, Federal University of Technology, Ikot Abasi, Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria *Corresponding author: nicodemusmkpuma@gmail.com Abstract Background: African hantaviruses remain among the least characterized members of the family Hantaviridae, with fragmented genomic data limiting our understanding of their evolutionary relationships, host associations, and geographic structuring. Here, we investigated the integrated continent-wide phylogenomic structure of African hantaviruses using all three coding genomic segments. Methods: We compiled and curated 281 full-length and partial coding sequences representing the L segment (n = 166), M segment (n = 48), and S segment (n = 67) from 13 African countries, alongside representative global reference strains. Temporal signal was evaluated using root-to-tip regression analysis. Segment-specific phylogenetic reconstructions were performed to characterize host-associated and geographic structuring. Additionally, pairwise tanglegram comparisons of the L, M, and S phylogenies were constructed to evaluate topological congruence and identify potential signals of genetic reassortment. Results: Root-to-tip regressions revealed weak temporal signal across the L (R2 = 0.069), M (R2 = 0.021), and S ( R2 = 0.046) datasets, precluding reliable molecular- clock inference. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated pronounced host-associated and geographic structuring across all three segments. Rodent, shrew, and bat-associated hantaviruses formed distinct evolutionary clades, with bat and shrew-borne lineages occupying basal, divergent positions relative to rodent-associated viruses. Endemic African hantaviruses exhibited marked regional clustering, forming distinct Malagasy, East African, and West African assemblages, whereas Senegalese, Beninese, and Malian sequences clustered within globally distributed, Rattus-associated Seoul orthohantavirus lineages. Comparative analyses highlighted complementary phylogenetic signals: the L segment provided a robust framework for resolving deep evolutionary relationships, the M segment offered clear discrimination among closely related host and geographic groups, and the S segment consistently recovered primary lineage boundaries. Pairwise tanglegrams demonstrated substantial topological concordance among segments highest between L and M with localized incongruences primarily in the L–S comparison restricted to closely related terminal taxa, consistent with but not definitive evidence of reassortment Conclusions: African hantaviruses display strong host-associated and geographic structuring, with major evolutionary relationships broadly conserved across all three genomic segments. These findings provide an integrated continent-wide phylogenomic framework, establishing a foundation for future genomic surveillance, evolutionary studies, and One Health strategies across Africa. papers.title: Predictive Surveillance for Andes Virus Transmission in the Americas.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations in conventional, case-based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person-to-person transmission. In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.
papers.journal: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene

In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

analysis.background: Recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks have refocused attention on anthropogenic environmental change as a driver of zoonotic emergence (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The commentary highlights human-driven deforestation, agricultural expansion, land‑use change, and ecosystem degradation as disruptors of wildlife‑livestock‑human interfaces that facilitate spillover, and proposes the One Health framework as a unifying strategy (A2, A3, A6).
analysis.current_state: Current evidence links habitat alteration to Ebola and hantavirus emergence, and predictive models indicate that EVD geographic risk will likely expand under present socioeconomic trends (A3, A4).
analysis.gaps: Key uncertainties remain regarding the quantitative impact of specific land‑use practices on spillover risk and the transition from reactive outbreak response to proactive prevention (A5).
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize integrated ecological and epidemiological surveillance, modeling of land‑use impacts, and multisectoral One Health interventions to mitigate environmental determinants of zoonoses (A5, A6).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks have refocused attention on anthropogenic environmental change as a driver of zoonotic emergence (A1). Main directions: Human-driven deforestation, agricultural expansion, land‑use change, and ecosystem degradation disrupt wildlife‑livestock‑human interfaces, facilitating spillover, and the One Health framework is proposed as a unifying strategy (A2, A3, A6). Current state: Evidence links habitat alteration to Ebola and hantavirus emergence, and predictive models forecast expanding EVD risk under current socioeconomic trends (A3, A4). Gaps: Uncertainty persists about the quantitative impact of specific land‑use practices on spillover and the shift from reactive to preventive responses (A5). Future research: Integrated ecological‑epidemiological surveillance, land‑use impact modeling, and multisectoral One Health interventions are needed to address environmental determinants of zoonoses (A5, A6).

papers.title_zh: 近期埃博拉病毒及汉坦病毒疫情的人为驱动因素:一体化健康视角

analysis_zh.background: 近期埃博拉病毒病及汉坦病毒疫情重新将注意力聚焦于人为环境变化作为人畜共患病出现的驱动因素 (A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 评论指出,人为导致的森林砍伐、农业扩张、土地利用变化和生态系统退化破坏了野生动物‐家畜‐人类交界面,促进病毒溢出,并提出“一体健康”框架作为统一策略 (A2, A3, A6)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 现有证据将栖息地改变与埃博拉及汉坦病毒的出现关联,预测模型显示,在当前社会经济趋势下,埃博拉病毒病的地理风险可能扩大 (A3, A4)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 关于特定土地利用实践对溢出风险的定量影响以及从被动疫情响应向主动预防转变的关键不确定性仍然存在 (A5)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应优先开展综合生态与流行病学监测、土地利用影响建模以及多部门“一体健康”干预,以减轻环境因素对人畜共患病的驱动作用 (A5, A6)。

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, presenting with fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak; its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis, creating diagnostic challenges (A1, A2).
analysis.methods: A single 33‑year‑old male patient was evaluated; clinical data, contrast‑enhanced CT imaging, laboratory tests, and whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) were performed to identify the pathogen (A3, A4, A6, A7).
analysis.results: The patient had profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10^9/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, and imaging showing peripancreatic/retroperitoneal exudation with mild pancreatic changes and bilateral pleural effusion; mNGS detected high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (A5, A6, A7). The patient recovered fully after supportive care, IV immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment, with normal pancreatic morphology on pre‑discharge ultrasound (A8, A9).
analysis.contribution: The report demonstrates that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can clinically and radiologically mimic severe acute pancreatitis, highlighting thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreatic parenchyma as diagnostic clues, and shows that mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation to guide appropriate management (A10, A11).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based on a single case report abstract only, limiting generalizability and preventing assessment of broader epidemiology or causality (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by orthohantaviruses can mimic acute pancreatitis, complicating diagnosis (A1, A2). Methods: A 33‑year‑old man was assessed with clinical labs, contrast CT, and whole‑blood mNGS (A3, A4, A6, A7). Results: He exhibited thrombocytopenia (29 × 10^9/L), renal impairment, retroperitoneal exudation, mild pancreatic changes, pleural effusion, and high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus by mNGS; he recovered fully with supportive care (A5, A6, A7, A8, A9). Contribution: The case shows Seoul orthohantavirus can imitate severe pancreatitis, with specific diagnostic clues and mNGS facilitating early confirmation and proper treatment (A10, A11). Limitations: Single‑patient abstract limits broader inference (abstract_only).

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热,模拟重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及通过mNGS确认病原

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种由 正汉坦病毒es 引起的人畜共患疾病,表现为发热、血小板减少、肾功能受损和毛细血管渗漏;其非典型表现可与急性胰腺炎极为相似,导致诊断挑战(A1, A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名33岁男性患者进行评估;收集临床资料,进行增强CT影像、实验室检查以及全血宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)以鉴定病原体(A3, A4, A6, A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现严重血小板减少(最低值 29 × 10^9/L)、进行性肾功能受损、血尿、蛋白尿,影像显示胰周/腹膜后渗出伴轻度胰腺改变及双侧胸腔积液;mNGS 检测到高拷贝首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒(A5, A6, A7)。患者经支持治疗、静脉免疫球蛋白和对症治疗后完全恢复,出院前超声显示胰腺形态正常(A8, A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本报告表明首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染在临床和影像上可模拟重症急性胰腺炎,血小板减少、肾脏受累及胰腺实质保持完整是诊断线索,并显示 mNGS 能早期确认病原体以指导适当治疗(A10, A11)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究仅基于单例病例报告摘要,限制了结果的普遍性,且无法评估更广泛的流行病学或因果关系(abstract_only)。

papers.title: Integrated in Silico Method for Virtual Screening and Interaction Profiling of Repurposed and Natural Inhibitor Candidates Against the Rdrp of the Newly Reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 Orthohantavirus
papers.abstract: Introduction: The rapid release of complete viral genome sequences enables early computational prioritization of antiviral candidates before experimental screening becomes available. Objectives: This study evaluated the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp; L protein) of the newly reported ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026 orthohantavirus as an antiviral drug-design target. Methods: The L-segment-derived RdRp sequence was obtained from the public Virological.org report, modeled with AlphaFold, inspected against the NCBI Conserved Domain Database, and submitted to CB-Dock2 for binding-cavity prediction. The predicted pocket (X = 5.872, Y = 29.895, Z = -5.566) was used for DrugRep screening of 100 FDA-approved/repurposed and 100 natural TCMML compounds, which were then independently rescored with KDeep. Results: In the repurposed library, DB00511 and DB11581 gave the strongest DrugRep scores (-10.2), whereas DB00864 gave the highest KDeep pIC50 (7.1249); consensus ranking prioritized DB00511, DB00390 and DB01396. In the natural-product library, T0295 scored best with DrugRep (-9.8) and T8166 with KDeep (7.3537); consensus ranking prioritized T8166, T0295, T6473 and T3809. Interaction analysis supported these candidates through recurrent hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic contacts, including GLU129, SER157, THR170, ALA1463, TRP1464, ARG1544 and GLU1545. Conclusions: The combined DrugRep-KDeep-interaction workflow provides a rational computational shortlist for downstream redocking, molecular dynamics, ADMET profiling and experimental prioritization.

papers.title: A Case Report of Hantavirus Capillary Leak Syndrome in the Southwestern United States.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. We report the case of a previously healthy 20-year-old man who initially presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive weakness after occupational exposure on a ranch in southwestern Arizona. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. In endemic areas with rodent exposure history, hemoconcentration and thrombocytopenia, along with signs of volume overload and rapidly progressive acute respiratory failure, should raise suspicion for hantavirus infection. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control.

papers.title: Hantavirus on a Cruise Ship: What COVID-19 Taught Us.
papers.abstract: Delayed recognition of the mechanics of aerosol transmission-the primary mode of spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-at the beginning of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic led to inadequate early recommendations regarding nonpharmaceutical interventions and poor initial messaging about how to reduce infection risk. We highlight key epidemiological details of Andes virus (ANDV) transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and during prior reported outbreaks with confirmed person-to-person spread in Argentina, which, together, suggest aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of transmission of ANDV between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissible environmental settings.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
